name: Facet
text:
Build the Excava interface in Figma as a clickable prototype first. It lets us test navigation, layout, and user flow without writing code, so we catch UX flaws early. The trade-off is slower feedback on performance and API integration, but clarity beats speed here.

Then ship a live HTML/CSS prototype tonight with real API calls. It forces us to solve real data problems now, not later, and proves the interface works end-to-end. The trade-off is rough edges in visual polish, but liveliness beats perfection.

name: Pane
text: Figma traps us in a static illusion—users will expect the interface to feel alive, not just clickable. A live HTML/CSS demo tonight forces us to confront real performance and API integration trade-offs now, not later. Ship the live prototype first; the Figma version can wait.

name: Facet
text:
Ship the live HTML/CSS prototype tonight. Real API calls expose performance bottlenecks and API quirks now, not later—this is the only way to test whether the interface feels alive and responsive under real conditions. The trade-off is rougher UX in early iterations, but clarity on what needs fixing beats polished mockups that hide problems.

name: Pane
text: Pane: Shipping a live HTML/CSS prototype tonight risks shipping a fragile artifact that looks broken under real API load, wasting tonight’s effort. A better alternative is to mock the API with realistic delays and errors in a controlled demo—this tests responsiveness without exposing us to live system failures. The argument settles when we see whether the mock demo reveals the same UX flaws as a real one.
